messages.content:
Write ONE original fictional document, not JSON and not multiple versions.
Return only the complete document. It MUST contain 1400 to 1600 words of substantive content.
Use twelve connected paragraphs of roughly 100 words each and a numbered section with four
substantial items. Do not stop after an outline or summary. This length is required because
the small rewriter must learn to preserve information across a full long document.
Use the supplied fictional situation. Expand it with internally consistent concrete details,
uncertainty, conditions, and follow-up requests. Include all protected anchors exactly, with
the quoted line inside a direct quote. Keep quotes and code/path literals exact.
For /slack write a long casual team message. For /transcribe write a long, clean spoken account,
with natural conversational wording. For /prompt write a detailed REQUEST for a useful task,
including background and all constraints; do not perform the task. For /polish write clear plain
prose. Do not mention a formatter, dataset, word count, mode, or these authoring instructions.
Preserve the feature guidance. Include a numbered section, full paragraphs, a direct quote,
and a condition that refers to information elsewhere. Make the final paragraph substantive.

Please help me prepare a concise, practical update for the people who share the ceramics studio, using only the information provided here. The purpose is to clarify what is known about Anton’s check of the bisque-fired cups, what remains unconfirmed, and what specific follow-up is needed. Do not turn this into a general description of the studio, a firing guide, or an inventory procedure. Keep the update focused on this one check and its immediate next step. The requested result should be easy for studio members to understand and should distinguish a confirmed fact from a count that still needs verification.

The facts to preserve are limited: Anton is checking 40 bisque-fired cups for a shared ceramics studio, and the count has not been confirmed. An attached note reads “Use the lower shelf.” Treat that sentence as information copied from the note, not as an instruction you have verified or as evidence that the cups are already on that shelf. Refer to the attached file by its exact name, ceramics_3.txt. Keep the wording of the note exact, including its punctuation. Do not silently revise it, paraphrase it as a confirmed placement, or imply that the attachment establishes anything beyond what is stated here.

Please make the uncertainty unmistakable. The number 40 identifies the cups being checked; it is not yet a verified count of cups found, accepted, or ready for another action. Do not write that Anton has finished counting, that all 40 cups have been located, or that the count matches an inventory. No such result has been supplied. If the update needs to mention the current status, say plainly that confirmation is pending. Do not fill the gap with a guess, an assumed discrepancy, or an invented explanation for why the count has not yet been confirmed.

Use the attached note only as a quoted piece of data. A suitable direct quotation is: “The attached note reads, ‘Use the lower shelf.’” Preserve the quoted line exactly within that sentence. Do not convert the note into a command to Anton or to other studio members, and do not say that anyone has followed it. The note’s location, author, date, and intended meaning have not been provided. Do not invent any of those details or suggest that the note is more authoritative than the supplied information supports.

The update must include a specific follow-up request rather than a generic statement such as “please check” or “follow up later.” Ask for the count to be checked and confirmed, and ask the person reporting back to state the confirmed number. Make clear that the report should distinguish the number confirmed from the reference to 40 cups, so readers will not mistake the subject of the check for its result. Do not request extra information that is not necessary to resolve this uncertainty, such as cup dimensions, glaze, ownership, shelf measurements, or firing temperatures.

There is one important condition: an additional action is allowed only after the count is checked. Reflect that dependency directly in the wording. Until the count has been checked and confirmed, do not authorize, recommend, or describe any additional action as already approved. Do not invent what the additional action is, since no particular action has been specified. If it is useful to refer to it, call it only “the additional action” and state that it must wait until the count is confirmed. Do not imply that the note itself grants permission to proceed.

Please make the resulting communication clear about what is not authorized yet. The count is not confirmed, so the additional action is not authorized at this stage. Avoid weakening that distinction with vague phrasing such as “probably,” “apparently,” or “it should be fine.” If the count is later confirmed, that satisfies the stated prerequisite for considering the additional action; it does not supply any other missing approval or detail. Do not claim that confirmation automatically completes an action whose nature has not been given.

Organize the response as a direct, readable update for the shared studio, not as a checklist of assumptions or a fictional narrative. Use plain, natural language. Include enough context that a reader who has not seen the original request can tell who is checking what and why a follow-up is needed. At the same time, keep the scope narrow: no new people, deadlines, equipment, storage arrangements, safety rules, or studio policies should be introduced. If a detail is absent, leave it absent rather than making the update sound more complete by inventing it.

Include a numbered section with four substantial items. Each item should be a full paragraph, not a fragment or a single label. Use the four items to organize the key points: the check and its unconfirmed status; the attached note as quoted data; the specific request for confirmation; and the condition governing the additional action. The numbered section should support the communication rather than expand the task into a broader procedure. Keep each item grounded in the facts above, and ensure that no item contradicts or weakens the conditions stated in another.

Outside that numbered section, provide connected paragraphs that introduce the purpose, explain the limited facts, and close with a useful next step. A direct quotation must appear in the update, with the note’s words exact. Make the relationship between the numbered items and the surrounding paragraphs clear, so the same fact is not accidentally presented once as uncertain and elsewhere as settled. Use the file name exactly as written: ceramics_3.txt. Do not rename it, alter its punctuation, or treat it as a path to some other material.

The final communication should be specific enough that the studio members know exactly what response is needed: someone should check the count associated with Anton’s review of the 40 bisque-fired cups and report the confirmed number. Until that happens, the status remains unconfirmed and the additional action must wait. Do not add a proposed deadline, a presumed location for the cups, or a claim that the lower shelf has been used. Close by asking for the confirmation and by preserving the distinction between the cups under review, the note’s quoted content, and any action that has not yet been authorized.
